summaries.example: Maya and Leo enjoy building models together. Maya feels happy when Leo succeeds, helps when he is stuck, and Leo does the same for her. They are not friends only because they need help or because the activity is fun. Their friendship includes caring about each other and wanting to spend time together.
summaries.summary: Friendship is more than liking someone or enjoying the same games. Philosophers describe it as a personal relationship in which each person cares about the other for that person’s own sake. Friends often share trust, feelings, interests, conversations, and activities. These parts can come in different amounts: some friendships are casual, while others are very close. A friendship can help people enjoy life, understand themselves, and grow. But friendship also raises hard questions. Should friends always take each other’s side? What should happen when helping a friend would be unfair or harmful? Philosophers also ask whether friendship is valuable only because it gives us happiness and help, or whether the friendship itself has value. The entry explains several views without choosing one final answer.
key_ideas: Friends care about one another for the other person’s sake.
Friendship usually includes closeness, trust, and knowing important things about each other.
Friends spend time doing things together, and the activity is part of the relationship.
Philosophers disagree about how much friends should influence one another and how friendship should fit with duties to everyone.
summaries.why_it_matters: Friendship affects how people feel, what they do, and who they become. Thinking about friendship can help us notice the difference between a friend and someone who is merely useful. It can also help us think carefully about loyalty, honesty, fairness, and the ways friends shape one another.

important_terms.definition: A relationship in which two people care about each other as individuals and share some part of their lives.
Caring about someone because that person matters, not only because they can help you.
A feeling of closeness and trust between people.
Doing something with another person because spending time together matters, not just because it is useful.

questions_to_think_about: Can two people be friends if they never spend time together?
Is a person still a good friend when they disagree with you?
Should a friend help you do something wrong?
What makes one particular friend special and not easily replaceable?

summaries.example: Suppose Elena and Sam have been friends for years. Elena values Sam’s judgment and sometimes changes her plans after discussing them with him; Sam does the same with her. They volunteer together partly because they care about the cause, but also because doing it together matters to them. If Sam begins supporting a harmful plan, Elena may have a special reason to challenge him rather than simply agree. Their case illustrates mutual concern, intimacy, shared activity, and the possible tension between loyalty and morality.
summaries.summary: The entry treats friendship as a distinctively personal relationship grounded in reciprocal concern for each friend as an individual, together with some degree of intimacy. This distinguishes friendship from one-sided love, and it also leaves open difficult boundaries between friendship, family relationships, and romantic love. Philosophical accounts commonly emphasize three elements: mutual caring, intimacy, and shared activity. Mutual caring involves emotional responsiveness to a friend’s successes and troubles and a disposition to promote the friend’s good for the friend’s sake. Theories disagree about whether this concern is based on recognizing a friend’s admirable qualities or on conferring special value on the person. Intimacy may involve disclosure and trust, shared interests and values, or a stronger mutual shaping of identity and practical judgment. The strongest versions risk reducing the independence of the individuals, while weaker versions may not explain friendship’s depth. Shared activity must be pursued partly for the sake of doing it together, not merely as a bargain for mutual advantage. The entry then considers friendship’s individual and social value, the difficulty of justifying one particular friendship without treating friends as replaceable, and the relationship between friendship’s special duties and impartial moral theories. It presents disagreements among consequentialist, deontological, virtue-ethical, and other approaches rather than settling them.
key_ideas: Friendship is not simply reciprocal affection. It is a relationship involving interaction, concern for the other’s sake, and some form of intimacy.
Accounts of intimacy range from mutual self-disclosure and trust to shared values, mutual influence, shared deliberation, and an ideal of living a life together.
Shared activity is normally motivated partly by the relationship itself. Philosophers differ about what makes an activity genuinely shared.
Aristotelian discussions distinguish friendships based on pleasure, usefulness, and virtue; many contemporary accounts focus on virtue friendship as the fullest form.
Friendship may be valuable instrumentally, by helping people flourish, and intrinsically, as a valuable relationship or community in its own right.
Friendship creates special duties and therefore tests moral theories that demand impartiality. The source presents continuing debate about whether loyalty can conflict with morality.
summaries.why_it_matters: Friendship is philosophically important because it joins personal attachment, value, action, and morality. Friends can help one another understand their character and sustain difficult intellectual or moral activities. They can also influence each other’s values, sometimes supporting unconventional ideas that contribute to social change. At the same time, friendships may encourage favoritism or bias, and loyalty can appear to conflict with duties owed to strangers. Studying these tensions clarifies what it means to care for a particular person without losing sight of wider moral responsibilities.

important_terms.definition: A personal relationship in which each person is concerned for the other as that particular person, with some degree of intimacy and interaction.
Concern for a friend’s welfare for the friend’s sake, expressed through sympathetic responses and a readiness to act for the friend’s good.
The closeness of friendship, explained by different theories through disclosure, trust, shared values, empathy, influence, or a jointly lived life.
Joint pursuits undertaken partly for the sake of doing them with a friend, rather than merely as an exchange of benefits.
A relationship-based obligation owed to a particular person, such as a friend, rather than equally to everyone.
The property of being replaceable by a sufficiently similar alternative without loss of value; friendship appears to resist this idea because its history is particular.
A view that evaluates actions or rules by their consequences, usually by asking which produces the most overall good.
A moral view that emphasizes duties or principles binding on moral agents, rather than judging actions only by their results.

questions_to_think_about: Does friendship require that friends share important values, or can deep friendship include enduring disagreement?
Why might the history of a friendship make the friend non-replaceable?
When does allowing a friend to influence you enrich your autonomy, and when might it threaten it?
Can an impartial moral theory explain why a person has special reasons to help a friend?
How should friendship respond when loyalty to a friend conflicts with a moral duty?

summaries.example: Jordan and Priya have been friends since joining the school robotics club. They like solving problems together, but their friendship is not just a trade: Jordan does not help Priya only because she will later help him. Each wants the other to do well, shares worries and successes, and trusts the other’s advice. When Priya wants to copy answers for a contest, Jordan must decide whether being loyal means staying quiet or means telling her that the plan is wrong.
summaries.summary: The philosophical study of friendship asks what makes friendship different from liking, romance, family attachment, or cooperation. A central answer is that friendship is a relationship of reciprocal concern: each person cares about the other for that person’s own sake. Philosophers also commonly identify intimacy and shared activity. Intimacy may mean trusting self-disclosure, understanding what matters to the other person, sharing values, or allowing friends to interpret and influence one another. These proposals disagree about how close friendship should be. A very weak account may describe only acquaintances, while a very strong account may threaten each person’s independence. Shared activity is also important, but it must be more than a useful bargain. Friends engage in activities partly because they want to do them together. The entry discusses older distinctions among friendships of pleasure, utility, and virtue, noting a tension between benefiting from a relationship and caring for the friend’s sake. It also asks why friendship is valuable. Friendship may make life richer, help people understand themselves, support good activities, and contribute to society. Yet it can also produce favoritism and social bias. Finally, friendship challenges moral theories because friends appear to have special duties to one another. Philosophers disagree about whether these duties can sometimes outweigh impartial moral demands.
key_ideas: Philosophers usually see friendship as mutual: each friend cares about the other for the other’s sake.
Friendship is usually more than having fun together. It involves a relationship with trust, closeness, or shared understanding.
Some philosophers think friends become more alike; others think friends may be very different and actively help shape each other.
Friendships based mainly on pleasure or usefulness may be less complete than friendships grounded in character, although the distinctions are debated.
A particular friend seems special because of the shared history between the friends, creating a challenge for the idea that people are replaceable.
Friendship raises a conflict between special loyalty to friends and moral rules that seem to require treating everyone impartially.
summaries.why_it_matters: Friendship is part of ordinary life, but it is not philosophically simple. Friends influence our choices and character, give us reasons to help particular people, and may help us see ourselves more clearly. Thinking about friendship can make us more careful about loyalty: supporting a friend does not automatically mean supporting every action. It also helps explain why fairness to everyone and special care for close people can both seem important.

important_terms.definition: A personal relationship where both people care about each other as individuals and have meaningful interaction.
Concern for another person because that person matters, rather than only because of what the relationship provides.
A deeper closeness built through trust, understanding, and sometimes sharing personal information or values.
An activity pursued together partly because the people want to share it, not merely to exchange useful favors.
A reason or responsibility that comes from having a particular relationship, such as being someone’s friend.
The idea that one friend could be swapped for another similar person without losing anything important.
A theory that judges actions by results and asks which choice creates the most good overall.
A theory that judges actions by duties or rules that apply to moral agents.

questions_to_think_about: Can a friendship be genuine if it is based mostly on usefulness?
Do friends need similar values, or can difference strengthen a friendship?
Should a friend accept your advice simply because you are close?
Why might ending one friendship and choosing a supposedly better one seem morally troubling?
What should someone do when helping a friend would harm another person?
